extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, design patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and design patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO MPEP guidance on what constitutes a protectable design, how design patents differ from utility patents, and practice rules for design patent practitioners including signature and admission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claimed is the design for an article, not the article itself
rubrics_metrics.description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Cady (1916) and In re Zahn (CCPA 1980). Emphasizes that 35 U.S.C. 171 refers to the design for an article, inclusive of surface ornamentation and configuration. Use this framing when identifying claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design consists of visual characteristics embodied in or applied to an article
rubrics_metrics.description: The design for an article consists of the visual characteristics embodied in or applied to an article (configuration, surface ornamentation, or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since design is manifested in appearance, subject matter may relate to shape/configuration, surface ornamentation, or their combination. Use drawings/figures to show the visual characteristics that constitute the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must be inseparable from the article and cannot exist as an abstract scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of surface ornamentation; it must be a definite, preconceived thing, capable of reproduction and not merely the chance result of a method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re SurgiSil (Fed. Cir. 2021) and Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions (Fed. Cir. 2019) for limits on 'design per se.' Ensure claimed design is tied to an identified article of manufacture and is reproducible; avoid claiming a design in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent and agency practice support that design patents are granted only for a design applied to an article of manufacture (i.e., include the article identification in the claim). Draft claims and identifications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose distinction: utility patents protect function; design patents protect appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents protect the way an article is used and works (35 U.S.C. 101), while design patents protect the way an article looks (35 U.S.C. 171).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamental appearance includes shape/configuration or surface ornamentation, or both. Both types of patents may be obtained if invention resides in both utility and ornamentality—assess whether claimed subject matter is principally functional or ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length difference (utility v. design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of a utility patent (filed on/after June 8, 1995) is 20 years from U.S. filing date (or earliest related application per §§120/121/365/386); term of a design patent is 15 years from date of grant if filed on/after May 13, 2015 (14 years if filed before May 13, 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. 173 as amended. Use correct term calculations depending on filing/grant dates and applicable statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance fees: required for utility patents but not design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance fees are required for utility patents (see 37 CFR 1.20), while no maintenance fees are required for design patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise clients about long-term fee obligations: design patents do not require periodic maintenance payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim count: design applications include only a single claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications include only a single claim, while utility patent applications can have multiple claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft design applications with a single claim that properly identifies the article of manufacture and the design as shown in the drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction practice: mandatory in design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction between plural, distinct inventions is discretionary in utility patent applications, while it is mandatory in design patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must require restriction when multiple distinct designs are claimed; applicants should present a single design per application or use continuing practice as appropriate (see MPEP §1504.05).

rubrics_metrics.name: International filing path differs (PCT vs Hague)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application designating various countries may be filed for utility patents under the PCT, whereas an international design application designating various countries may be filed for design protection under the Hague Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP Chapter 2900 for international design application practice and choose the appropriate international route (PCT for utility, Hague for design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority period shorter for design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) can be obtained for utility patent filings up to 1 year after the first filing, whereas the period is only 6 months for design patent applications (see 35 U.S.C. 172).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan foreign filing strategy accordingly; missing the 6-month window may forfeit priority for design filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design applications cannot claim provisional benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patent applications may claim the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e), whereas design patent applications may not (see 35 U.S.C. 172 and 37 CFR 1.78(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on provisional filings to secure an effective filing date for design patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for Continued Examination (RCE) not available for design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A Request for Continued Examination (RCE) under 37 CFR 1.114 may only be filed in utility and plant applications under certain conditions; RCE is not available for design applications (see 37 CFR 1.114(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available continuing application practices (e.g., CPA under 37 CFR 1.53(d) when applicable) rather than RCE for design prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) practice available for design applications under chapter 16
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued prosecution application (CPA) practice under 37 CFR 1.53(d) is available for design applications filed under 35 U.S.C. chapter 16 (see 37 CFR 1.53(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When further prosecution is needed in a design case, evaluate CPA eligibility and procedures as the available route for continuing prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication: utility apps generally published; design apps under chapter 16 are not published
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patent applications filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 are subject to application publication under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(1)(A), whereas design applications filed under 35 U.S.C. chapter 16 are not subject to application publication (see 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design applicants should be aware that their applications are generally not published as utility applications are, which affects prior art/public notice considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default applicability of utility rules to design practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise provided, the rules for utility patents are equally applicable to design patent applications (35 U.S.C. 171 and 37 CFR 1.151 and 1.1061).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to utility patent rules where design-specific provisions do not provide otherwise; check cited statutes and regs for applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent practitioner signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent practitioner must indicate their design patent practitioner status by placing the word 'design' (in any format) adjacent to their handwritten signature or adjacent to the last forward slash of their S-signature; practitioners signing pursuant to §1.33 must supply their registration number as part of the S-signature or adjacent to it, with the hash character allowed only before the registration number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For every piece of correspondence requiring signature (with some exceptions), ensure the appropriate S-signature or handwritten signature formatting and inclusion of 'design' to make status clear on the record (37 CFR 1.4(d)(1)-(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent practitioner bar: limited practice and registration category
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective January 2, 2024, the USPTO created a separate design patent practitioner bar; design patent practitioners are registered under 37 CFR 11.6(d) and can only practice in design patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent practitioners registered to practice in all patent matters (§11.6(a)-(c)) can practice in design matters, but design-only registrants cannot sign papers in utility or plant applications. Power of attorney customer number rules may restrict cross-use between design and utility matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent practitioner admission/qualification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants to the design patent practitioner bar should have a bachelor's, master's, or doctorate degree in industrial design, product design, architecture, applied arts, graphic design, fine/studio arts, art teacher education, or an equivalent degree from an accredited institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modified scientific/technical requirements broaden admission for design practitioners; see Office of Enrollment and Discipline for more details and application procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competence and informing clients of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent practitioners, like all patent practitioners, are required to provide competent representation to their clients, which includes properly informing clients of practice limitations (see 37 CFR 11.101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design practitioners must communicate scope-of-practice limits (e.g., inability to practice in utility matters) as part of competent representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural resources and limitations on Office assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: A listing of registered patent attorneys and agents (including design patent attorneys and agents) is available online; the Office cannot aid in selecting a patent practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct applicants to the USPTO list or OED for locating practitioners and note that the Office will not recommend or select practitioners for applicants (see 37 CFR 1.31 and MPEP §401).
